title: Probability and Conditional Probability
subtitle: Master basic probability, two-way tables, conditional probability, and complementary events

sections.title: The Core Formula
sections.content:
Probability measures how likely an event is:

$$P(\text{event}) = \frac{\text{Number of favorable outcomes}}{\text{Total number of outcomes}}$$

- Probability is always between 0 and 1 (or 0% and 100%)
- $P = 0$: impossible; $P = 1$: certain; $P = 0.5$: 50-50

**On the SAT:** nearly every probability problem involves either a two-way table or a simple list of outcomes. The challenge is identifying the correct numerator and denominator.

sections.title: Example: Probability from a List
sections.problem: A bag contains 7 red, 4 white, 11 blue, and 8 green marbles. One marble is drawn at random. What is the probability of drawing a red marble?

sections.title: Example: Find a Missing Count from a Probability
sections.problem: There are 350 customers in theaters A, B, and C. P(theater A) = 0.48, P(theater B) = 0.40. How many customers are in theater C?
sections.tip: When multiple mutually exclusive groups are given, probabilities must add to 1. Find the missing probability first, then multiply by the total.

sections.title: Type 2: Probability from a Two-Way Table
Reading the Correct Cell
sections.content:
A two-way table shows counts for two categorical variables. SAT probability questions almost always ask you to:
1. Find the **numerator** — the count matching both conditions (the intersection cell)
2. Find the **denominator** — depends on whether it's a simple probability (grand total) or conditional (row/column total)

**Simple probability:** denominator = grand total
**Conditional probability:** denominator = total of the 'given' group

sections.title: Example: Read a Two-Way Table
sections.problem: A survey of 100 people shows: 40 own cats, 35 own dogs, 15 own both, and 30 own neither. If one person is selected at random, what is the probability they own a cat but not a dog?

steps.description: Cat only = own cat − own both = 40 − 15 = 25

sections.tip: For 'A but not B' questions: count(A but not B) = count(A) − count(A and B). Draw a Venn diagram if needed.

sections.title: The 'Given That' Changes the Denominator
sections.content:
**Conditional probability** $P(A \mid B)$ = probability of A **given** B has occurred:

$$P(A \mid B) = \frac{\text{Count of both A and B}}{\text{Count of B (the given group)}}$$

**How to recognize conditional probability in SAT language:**
- "Of the students who passed..." → condition is 'passed'
- "Given that the person is female..." → condition is 'female'
- "Among those who own dogs..." → condition is 'dog owners'

**Key:** the denominator changes from the grand total to the count of the **given group**.

sections.title: Example: Conditional from a Table
sections.problem:
A table shows 48 Himalayan kittens by coat color and eye color:
- 14 are chocolate-coated
- Of the 14 chocolate, 8 have deep blue eyes

What fraction of chocolate-coated kittens have deep blue eyes?

steps.description: The condition is 'chocolate-coated' → denominator = 14 (total chocolate kittens)

sections.tip: The phrase 'of the chocolate kittens' tells you the denominator is 14, NOT the grand total of 48.

sections.title: Example: Conditional vs. Simple Probability — Spot the Difference
sections.problem:
A school survey shows 200 students: 80 are in the band, 60 are in sports, 30 are in both, 90 are in neither.

(A) What is P(band)?
(B) What is P(band | sports)?

steps.description: (B) Conditional: given 'sports' → denominator = 60 (sports students). Both band AND sports = 30

sections.tip: Compare: 40% of ALL students are in band, but 50% of SPORTS students are also in band. The 'given' group narrows your universe.

sections.title: P(not A) = 1 − P(A)
sections.content:
The probability that an event does NOT happen:
$$P(\text{not A}) = 1 - P(A)$$

Use this when it's easier to count what you **don't** want and subtract from 1.

**Example:** P(at least one success) = 1 − P(no successes)

sections.title: Example: 'Neither' Probability
sections.problem: A bag has 7 red, 4 white, 33 blue, and 33 yellow cubes. What is the probability of selecting a cube that is neither blue nor yellow?

steps.description: Total = 7 + 4 + 33 + 33 = 77. Not blue and not yellow = red + white = 7 + 4 = 11

sections.tip: For 'neither A nor B': just count the items that are not A and not B directly. Complement shortcut: P(neither) = 1 − P(blue or yellow) = 1 − (66/77) = 11/77 = 1/7.

sections.title: Example: 'At Least One' Using Complement
sections.problem: A teacher randomly selects 2 students from a class of 10 (4 boys, 6 girls). What is the probability that at least one girl is selected? (Assume without replacement.)

steps.description: Use complement: P(at least 1 girl) = 1 − P(no girls)
P(both boys): P(1st is boy) × P(2nd is boy | 1st is boy)

sections.tip: Whenever you see 'at least one,' use the complement: 1 − P(none). Counting directly (exactly 1 girl + exactly 2 girls) is much harder.

sections.title: Example: Build the Table from Information Given
sections.problem: A study of 200 people recorded whether they exercise regularly (yes/no) and whether they have high blood pressure (yes/no). 90 exercise regularly. Of those who exercise, 20 have high blood pressure. Of those who don't exercise, 60 have high blood pressure. Complete the table and find P(high BP | does not exercise).

steps.description: Fill in the table: Total = 200. Exercises = 90, doesn't exercise = 110
steps.math: \text{Exercises: 20 high BP, 70 no high BP} \qquad \text{No exercise: 60 high BP, 50 no high BP}

steps.description: P(high BP | no exercise): denominator = 110 (those who don't exercise)

sections.tip: Build the full table even if the question only asks for one value — having all cells filled in prevents errors with numerators and denominators.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: **Simple vs. conditional:** 'given [group]' means denominator = that group's total, NOT the grand total
**'A but not B':** count(A) − count(A and B)
**Complementary:** P(not A) = 1 − P(A) — use this for 'at least one' questions
**'At least one' shortcut:** P(at least 1) = 1 − P(none)
**Probabilities sum to 1:** use to find a missing category's probability

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Conditional probability: using grand total instead of the 'given' group's total
- 'A and B' vs. 'A | B': P(A and B) uses grand total as denominator; P(A | B) uses B's total
- Forgetting to fill in the whole table before answering
- For 'neither A nor B': trying to use 1 − P(A) − P(B) without accounting for overlap

sat_tips: The phrase 'of the [group]' (e.g., 'of the students who passed') always signals a conditional probability — change the denominator
For 'at least one' problems, use the complement: P(at least 1) = 1 − P(none)
When given probabilities that must sum to 1, find the missing probability first, then multiply by total to get count
Draw a Venn diagram for 'A but not B' and 'neither A nor B' problems — it prevents errors
